title: Give every worker of the settlement pool several pieces

blocks.text: The settlement job nets the day's trades on whatever `ForkJoinPool` the deployment hands it: two workers in staging, twelve in production. The big clients' trades sit together at the end of the day's file and take far longer to net than the rest, and in production the job runs about as long as it would on one thread, while most workers sit idle near the end.

The operations team has set the rule for how the day is cut up: each worker of the pool the job runs in gets between 32 and 64 pieces of a large day, and a batch of `minRows` trades or fewer is netted whole, because a piece that small isn't worth a task.

`SettlementJob` already halves the day until a range fits in one piece. Finish `leafSize(rows)` in `src/main/java/practice/SettlementJob.java`, which says how many trades one piece may hold. About two lines in total. The tests run the job on real pools of one to forty workers.

cases.says: the job's total is the sum of every trade's net amount, for any number of trades and any pool
a large day is netted in 32 to 64 pieces per worker, not one piece per worker
the number of pieces follows the parallelism of the pool the job runs in, not the machine's processor count
a batch of minRows trades or fewer is netted in one piece

origin.section: Uneven Work Needs Many More Leaves Than Workers

concepts: A started leaf is never shared, so uneven work needs leaves small enough that the costly items spread over many of them; one or four leaves per worker leave workers idle.
The number of leaves is sized from the parallelism of the pool the task runs in, not from the machine's processor count.
